title: CSS Custom Properties (Variables)
summary: **CSS custom properties** (`--name`) are author-defined, cascading, inheritable variables read with `var(--name, fallback)`. Unlike preprocessor variables, they live at runtime — they cascade, can be scoped per element, updated with JavaScript, and combined with `calc()` — making them the foundation of theming and dark mode.

subtopics.title: Declaring custom properties (--name)
subtopics.explanation: A custom property is any property whose name starts with two dashes, e.g. --brand: #3b82f6. Names are case-sensitive. The value can be almost anything — a color, length, or even a partial token — and it is not validated until used. They are declared inside a normal rule, most often on :root.

subtopics.title: Reading values with var() and fallbacks
subtopics.explanation: You read a custom property with var(--name). var() accepts an optional fallback used when the property is unset or invalid: var(--accent, #ccc). Fallbacks can even be other var() calls. If a var() resolves to an invalid value for the property, it triggers 'invalid at computed value time' and the property uses its inherited or initial value.

subtopics.title: :root scope vs local scope
subtopics.explanation: Declaring on :root (the html element) makes a variable available globally because custom properties inherit. Declaring on a specific element or class scopes the value to that element and its descendants, overriding the global one locally — the basis of component-level theming.

subtopics.title: Inheritance and the cascade
subtopics.explanation: Custom properties are inherited by default and participate in the cascade like any property, so specificity and source order decide which declaration wins, and descendants pick up the resolved value. This is why a variable set on a parent automatically flows to children unless re-declared.

subtopics.title: Theming and dark mode
subtopics.explanation: Define a set of semantic variables (--bg, --text, --surface) on :root, then override them under a class or a media query like prefers-color-scheme. Components reference only the variables, so switching themes is a single declaration block change — no rule duplication.

subtopics.title: Runtime updates via JavaScript
subtopics.explanation: Because custom properties are live, JavaScript can read and write them with element.style.setProperty('--x', value) or getComputedStyle. Updating a variable instantly restyles every rule that uses it — ideal for user-controlled themes, sliders, and animations driven by a single value.

subtopics.title: Combining with calc()
subtopics.explanation: Custom properties shine inside calc(): you can derive spacing scales, fluid sizes, and layouts from a few base tokens. Because the variable is resolved at computed-value time, calc() recomputes whenever the variable changes (including from JS).

subtopics.title: CSS variables vs Sass variables
subtopics.explanation: Sass ($var) variables are compile-time: they are substituted when the stylesheet is built and disappear from the output, so they cannot change at runtime, cascade, or be read by JS. CSS custom properties are runtime, cascading, inheritable, and DOM-aware. Use Sass vars for build-time constants and CSS vars for anything dynamic or themeable.

foundations.overview: CSS custom properties let you store a value once and reuse it everywhere with var(). Unlike preprocessor variables that vanish at build time, custom properties are real CSS entities: they cascade, inherit, can be scoped to any element, recomputed by calc(), and changed live from JavaScript or media queries. That runtime nature is what makes scalable theming, dark mode, and dynamic UI practical without duplicating rules.
foundations.formalDefinition: A CSS custom property is a property whose name begins with two hyphens (--*) that holds an author-defined value, accessed via the var() function. It is inherited by default, participates in the cascade, and is substituted into other declarations at computed-value time.
foundations.whyItMatters: Theming, dark mode, design tokens, component variants, and JS-driven interactions all rely on custom properties. They are increasingly common in interviews, especially the distinction from Sass variables and how var() fallbacks and scoping behave.
foundations.mentalModel: Think of a custom property as a named slot attached to an element that flows down to its descendants. var() reads the nearest slot value in the cascade; redeclaring the slot lower in the tree overrides it just for that subtree, like passing context down a component hierarchy.
foundations.browserPerspective: The browser stores custom properties largely as unparsed token streams, inheriting them down the tree. At computed-value time it substitutes var() references into the using declaration and then parses the result for that specific property; if the substituted value is invalid there, the property becomes invalid at computed-value time and falls back to inherited/initial.
foundations.realWorldUsage: Design-token systems, light/dark theming, per-component variants (--btn-bg), spacing/typographic scales via calc(), animation values driven from one variable, and JS-controlled user themes or sliders.
foundations.businessImpact: Centralized tokens make rebrands and dark mode fast and low-risk, improving accessibility and user preference support while reducing the cost of UI changes across a product.
foundations.engineeringImpact: Variables eliminate magic-number duplication, shrink CSS by removing repeated theme rules, and create a clean contract between design tokens and components, improving consistency and refactorability.
foundations.performanceImpact: Resolving custom properties is cheap, but changing a variable on a high-level element (e.g. :root) can trigger style recalculation across the whole subtree that uses it; scope updates as narrowly as possible for hot paths.
commonUseCases: Design tokens for color, spacing, and typography
Light/dark theming via :root overrides or prefers-color-scheme
JS-driven dynamic values: user themes, sliders, animations

commonMisconceptions.myth: CSS variables work just like Sass variables.
commonMisconceptions.reality: Sass variables are compile-time and disappear from output; CSS custom properties are runtime, cascade, inherit, and can be changed by JS and media queries.

commonMisconceptions.myth: A var() fallback is used whenever the value 'looks wrong'.
commonMisconceptions.reality: The fallback is used only when the property is unset/invalid at the var() call; an invalid SUBSTITUTED value instead makes the property invalid at computed-value time and falls back to inherited/initial, not the var() fallback.

codeLab.title: Build a themeable button with local overrides
codeLab.instructions: Define a base .btn using var() tokens, then create a .btn--danger modifier that overrides only the relevant variables (not the whole rule). Hint: redeclare --btn-bg inside .btn--danger so the inherited var() picks it up.
codeLab.expectedOutput: Two buttons styled by the same base rule — one default (indigo) and one danger (red) — differing only by an overridden variable.
hints: Set a default --btn-bg on .btn and reference it with background: var(--btn-bg).
The modifier only needs to redeclare --btn-bg; the base rule's var() will resolve to the new value.
This avoids repeating the whole background/padding rule per variant.

debuggingLab.title: Why is my variable empty?
debuggingLab.symptom: A button references var(--accent) but renders with no background color (transparent) instead of the brand color.
debuggingLab.errorAnalysis: The variable --accent is declared on .theme, but the button is not inside any .theme element, so it never inherits --accent. Since the property is unset and var() has no fallback, background resolves to its initial value (transparent). Custom properties only flow to descendants of the element they are declared on.
commonMistakes: Declaring a variable on a scope the consuming element is not inside of.
Omitting a var() fallback for variables that might be unset.
Assuming custom properties are global regardless of where they are declared (only :root is truly global).
debuggingLab.fixChallenge: Make the variable reach the button — either move the declaration to :root or add a sensible var() fallback.

theory.question: What are CSS custom properties and how do they differ from Sass variables?
theory.directAnswer: CSS custom properties are author-defined variables (--name) read with var() that exist at runtime: they cascade, inherit, can be scoped to any element, recomputed by calc(), and changed by JavaScript or media queries. Sass variables ($name) are compile-time — they are substituted when the stylesheet is built and don't exist in the output, so they can't cascade, be scoped at runtime, or be read/written by JS.

detailedExplanation.whatItIs: Native, inheritable CSS variables that live in the DOM and resolve at computed-value time.
detailedExplanation.whyItExists: To enable runtime theming, design tokens, and dynamic values without duplicating rules — things preprocessor variables can't do.
detailedExplanation.howItWorks: Declared as --name in a rule (often :root), inherited to descendants, and substituted into declarations via var() with an optional fallback.

theory.whyImportant: The runtime-vs-compile-time distinction is a frequent interview question and underpins modern theming.
theory.realWorldExample: Dark mode overrides --bg and --text under a .dark class, instantly restyling every component that uses those variables.

nestedTopics.title: Runtime vs compile-time
nestedTopics.explanation: CSS vars resolve in the browser; Sass vars are gone after build.

nestedTopics.title: Cascade and inheritance
nestedTopics.explanation: Custom properties inherit and obey specificity/source order.

nestedTopics.title: JS interop
nestedTopics.explanation: setProperty/getComputedStyle can read and update CSS vars live; Sass vars cannot.

followUps.question: Can you still use both Sass and CSS variables together?
followUps.answer: Yes — use Sass for build-time constants and logic, and emit CSS custom properties for anything that must change at runtime, like themes.

followUps.question: Are custom properties inherited by default?
followUps.answer: Yes; that's why declaring on :root makes them effectively global to all descendants.

theory.question: How does var() fallback work, and what is 'invalid at computed-value time'?
theory.directAnswer: var(--name, fallback) uses the fallback only when --name is not set (or is the guaranteed-invalid initial value) at that call. If the variable IS set but its substituted value is invalid for the property using it, the property becomes 'invalid at computed-value time' and falls back to its inherited or initial value — not to the var() fallback. So the fallback covers an unset variable, not a wrong-typed one.

detailedExplanation.whatItIs: Two distinct fallback behaviors: the explicit var() fallback and the invalid-at-computed-value-time rule.
detailedExplanation.whyItExists: Because custom properties are type-agnostic until used, the browser can only detect invalidity after substitution into a specific property.
detailedExplanation.howItWorks: var() substitutes the value into the declaration; the result is then parsed for that property. Unset variable -> use fallback; set-but-invalid result -> property uses inherited/initial.

theory.whyImportant: Misunderstanding this leads to confusing bugs where a fallback is expected but the property silently resets.
theory.realWorldExample: color: var(--accent, #64748b) shows gray if --accent is undefined, but if --accent: 10px (wrong type) the color resets to its inherited value, not gray.

nestedTopics.title: Explicit fallback
nestedTopics.explanation: The second argument of var() handles an unset variable.

nestedTopics.title: Invalid at computed-value time
nestedTopics.explanation: A set-but-invalid substituted value resets the property to inherited/initial.

nestedTopics.title: Type-agnostic storage
nestedTopics.explanation: Custom properties store tokens; type checking happens only at use.

followUps.question: How can you guard against invalid values?
followUps.answer: Use @property to register a custom property with a type and an initial value, which enables type checking and a guaranteed fallback.

scenario.question: You need a user-selectable accent color that updates the whole UI instantly when changed from a color picker. How do you architect it?
scenario.directAnswer: Define a single semantic variable like --accent on :root and have every component reference var(--accent). Then, on the color picker's change event, call document.documentElement.style.setProperty('--accent', value). Because custom properties are runtime and inherited, updating the one variable instantly restyles every rule that uses it — no re-rendering or rule duplication.

detailedExplanation.whatItIs: A runtime theming pattern driven by one cascading variable plus a JS write.
detailedExplanation.whyItExists: Custom properties are live DOM values, so changing them recomputes dependent styles automatically.
detailedExplanation.howItWorks: setProperty on :root updates the inherited value; the browser recomputes every var(--accent) usage in the affected subtree.

scenario.whyImportant: It demonstrates the key advantage over Sass variables and a common real-world theming requirement.

nestedTopics.title: Single source of truth
nestedTopics.explanation: One :root variable referenced everywhere keeps updates centralized.

nestedTopics.title: JS interop
nestedTopics.explanation: setProperty/getComputedStyle bridge CSS variables and scripts.

nestedTopics.title: Scope of recalc
nestedTopics.explanation: Updating :root recalculates the whole subtree using the variable.

followUps.question: How do you persist the user's choice?
followUps.answer: Save the value in localStorage and re-apply it with setProperty on page load before paint.

coding.question: Write CSS that defines a base spacing token and derives a small and large spacing from it using calc(), then build a dark-mode override.
coding.thoughtProcess: I want a single source of truth for spacing and color. I define --space on :root and derive --space-sm and --space-lg with calc() so the scale stays proportional. Colors go through semantic variables (--bg, --text) so a dark theme is just an override block under a class — no rule duplication. Everything resolves at runtime, so the override flows to all descendants.
coding.lineByLine: :root defines the base --space plus derived --space-sm (half) and --space-lg (double) via calc(), keeping the scale proportional. --bg and --text are semantic color tokens. .theme-dark overrides only the color variables, so any .panel inside it flips to dark automatically. .panel consumes the tokens, so changing a base variable rescales or recolors everything that references it.

alternativeApproaches.title: prefers-color-scheme media query
alternativeApproaches.explanation: Override the color variables based on the OS theme instead of a class, for automatic dark mode.

followUps.question: Why derive sizes with calc() instead of hardcoding them?
followUps.answer: A single base token drives the whole scale, so adjusting --space rescales every derived value consistently and avoids magic numbers.

productionDeepDive.architecture: Custom properties are the runtime layer of a design-token system: build tools may emit them from a token source, and components reference only semantic variables (--bg, --text, --space). Themes and variants become override blocks rather than duplicated rules, cleanly separating tokens from component CSS.
productionDeepDive.performance: Resolving var() is cheap, but mutating a variable high in the tree (e.g. :root) recalculates styles for the entire subtree that consumes it. For hot paths and animations, scope variable changes as narrowly as possible and prefer animating registered (@property) numeric variables.
productionDeepDive.security: Writing custom properties from untrusted input via inline styles or setProperty can be an injection vector (CSS values can reference urls); constrain and validate dynamic values, and treat variable values as data, not trusted code.
productionDeepDive.scaling: Establish a tiered token system (primitive -> semantic -> component variables) so large teams override at the right layer; document the contract and avoid leaking implementation-detail variables into component APIs.
productionDeepDive.maintainability: Name variables by intent (--surface, not --gray-100 in component code), provide var() fallbacks for resilience, and consider @property to register types and initial values so invalid updates fail safely.
productionDeepDive.observability: DevTools shows computed custom-property values and where they are inherited from, making it easy to trace which scope a var() resolves to and to debug unexpected overrides.

caseStudies.problem: Needed runtime theming (light/dark, brand variants) without shipping duplicate stylesheets.
caseStudies.solution: Emitted design tokens as CSS custom properties consumed by all components, with themes as override blocks.
caseStudies.tradeoffs: Root-level updates can be costly to recalc; teams scope overrides and register hot variables.
caseStudies.lessons: A semantic custom-property layer makes theming a one-block change instead of a rewrite.

keyTakeaways: Custom properties (--name) are runtime, cascading, inheritable variables read with var() — unlike compile-time Sass variables.
var(--name, fallback) uses the fallback only when the variable is unset; a set-but-invalid value makes the property fall back to inherited/initial instead.
Declare on :root for global tokens; redeclare on an element/class to scope (and override) values locally.
Because they are live, JavaScript (setProperty) and media queries can update variables and instantly restyle everything that uses them.
Combine custom properties with calc() to derive scales from a few base tokens — the foundation of theming and dark mode.
